facts.fact: Described in 2009 by Franklin F. Snelson Jr., Trevor J. Krabbenhoft and Joseph M. Quattro in the Bulletin of the Florida Museum of Natural History.
Before its description it was confused with its sister species, Elassoma okefenokee.
Molecular data at two gene loci support separating it from E. okefenokee.
The species name honours Carter R. Gilbert, former Curator of Fishes at the Florida Museum of Natural History.
It has four preopercular canal pores, against three in E. okefenokee.
It usually has seven anal fin rays, while E. okefenokee usually has eight.
Its body is slightly less deep and its dorsal and anal fins slightly smaller than in E. okefenokee.
The sides carry dark brown bars, with many black specks and spots on the head and body.
Two large cream-coloured spots sit at the base of the tail fin.
The lips are light-coloured.
The IUCN lists it as Least Concern, assessed on 29 November 2011.
The Aquarium Wiki entry lists a lifespan of 4 to 5 years, longer than the one to two years a breeder reports.
Fishipedia lists a longevity of 8 years.
It lives in Gulf of Mexico drainages of northwestern Florida and extreme southwestern Georgia, USA.
Its range runs from the Waccasassa River west to Choctawhatchee Bay and includes the lower Suwannee River drainage.
The Florida Museum lists the Choctawhatchee, Apalachicola, Ochlockonee, Suwannee and Lake Okeechobee drainages and minor Gulf tributaries.
The type locality is near Tallahassee, Florida.
An aquarium wholesaler gives its origin as Florida and Alabama.
A hobbyist collected wild fish from a tributary of the Wacissa River in Jefferson County, Florida.
It lives in swamps, sloughs, ditches and the backwaters of small streams.
It is usually found near vegetation or woody debris.
It usually occupies slackwater areas with dense aquatic vegetation and leaf litter.

A biotope aquarium modelled on a small, slow-flowing tributary of the Wacissa River was judged a fairly accurate depiction of Elassoma habitat by expert Fritz Rohde, except that rocks do not occur in the Florida panhandle.
The species is traded as an ornamental fish.
A German wholesaler has offered captive-bred specimens, to wholesale customers only.
A keeper's wild-caught fish needed three rounds of praziquantel for intestinal parasites.
It is short-lived, so a breeding colony is needed to keep numbers up.
One breeder started with a 10-gallon (about 38 L) tank and later kept a colony in a 55-gallon (about 208 L) tank.
A pair bred in a 5-gallon (about 19 L) Fluval Edge.
One keeper spawns it in tanks under 2.5 gallons (about 9.5 L) and grows fry in a 4-gallon (about 15 L) tank.
The Aquarium Wiki gives a minimum tank of 38 litres (10 US gallons).
Fishipedia recommends a minimum of 30 litres.
Plants or decorations that break sight lines allow several coloured males to live together.
It has been spawned in both pH 6.5, 0 DH water and pH 7.5, 17 DH water.
Spawning has been reported in water of 0 DH and 20 DH, suggesting tolerance of a wide hardness range.
One breeder saw no apparent difference between keeping it with or without a heater.
A wholesaler recommends room temperature of 16–24 °C with no additional heating.
A pair bred without a heater at room temperatures of 68–80 °F (20–27 °C).
One spawning tank was slightly alkaline over crushed coral, in a house at about 68 °F (20 °C), with no filter.
A biotope tank for wild-caught fish ran at 24 °C and pH 7.2 with slow flow.
The Aquarium Wiki lists hardness of 5 to 12 °d.
It needs a zero-current resting area, though it will play in strong current.
In the wild it feeds mainly on tiny insects, crustaceans and worms.
In aquaria it takes blackworms, cut frozen bloodworms and cultured grindal worms.
When one colony was switched to flake food, some fish starved and fry production stopped.
Daily live foods used in one breeding tank were mostly grindal worms, plus daphnia and mosquito larvae.
Fry eat microworms, rotifers and microfauna.
Four-week-old fry cannot eat adult Daphnia but do eat baby Daphnia, along with green water, algae and biofilm microorganisms.
It is an ambush predator that hides under cover and pounces on live food.
Males are very territorial and chase rivals out of their line of sight.
Colour shows mood: stressed, submissive or unwell fish turn pale and clear.
Hand-feeding tames the fish so that they come out of cover when people are present.
Males dance by wiggling their fins to show their blue iridescence, then hold completely still for a few seconds.
Large males are black with bright iridescent blue bars on the side of the body and below the eye.
Breeding females often have blue dashes below and behind the eye, which female E. okefenokee lack.
Females stay smaller than males.
In the wild in Florida, it spawns from mid to late winter until the summer rainy season starts, when water is low and food is dense (a keeper's account).
In aquaria, males need dense living or artificial plants to claim as territory, and guard the spawn site until the eggs hatch.
In aquaria, males court females into a clump of plants, and eggs usually fall through the plants to the substrate.
In aquaria, eggs hatch in 3 to 4 days.
Once the fry hatch, the male is ready to court again.
Well-fed aquarium colonies breed continuously.
The eggs and young are tiny, which makes rearing somewhat difficult.
In aquaria, fry hug the bottom and were raised on banana worms and small organisms from daphnia buckets.
One keeper removed the parents once eggs appeared and raised fry on live Daphnia and Cyclops from an outdoor pond, which also brought in algae.
Leaving the light on 16 to 18 hours a day fed algae and green water and gave one keeper his fastest fry growth.
At four weeks, fry vary greatly in size and their markings are starting to show; the largest may soon eat the smallest siblings.
Aquatic isopods in one spawning tank were observed not to touch viable eggs.
One keeper advises leaving ramshorn snails out of spawning tanks because they would probably eat eggs.
Hatch rates did not change significantly when embryos were exposed to different concentrations of formalin, iodine or hydrogen peroxide in culture trials.
